title: Nvidia partners with 8 Australian firms for 2GW AI buildout
text:
Nvidia $NVDA announced on Thursday that it is partnering with eight Australian data center and cloud companies to expand AI computing capacity in the country, targeting a buildout of up to 2 gigawatts by 2027. Australia's existing computing capacity is 1.6 GW, per Reuters , which cited figures from analysts DC Byte, putting the planned expansion on track to more than double the nation's current load.
Nvidia listed eight partners in the announcement: Firmus, Sharon AI, IREN, Megaport, ResetData, CDC, NEXTDC, and AirTrunk. The participating companies will operate what Nvidia calls AI factories — a label the company applies to deployments that integrate every layer from physical infrastructure and compute to networking, software, and reference designs, all anchored to its DSX platform. Nvidia said it will supply the DSX platform, accelerated computing, networking, software, and ecosystem support.
"AI factories turn energy into intelligence — the essential resource of the AI economy," Raj Mirpuri, vice president of global AI clouds and infrastructure ecosystem at Nvidia , said in a statement.
The partners are at varying stages of buildout. IREN is applying the DSX architecture to its 800-megawatt Bundey campus in South Australia. CDC said its existing footprint across Australia and New Zealand exceeds 550 megawatts, and that an additional 800 megawatts is currently being developed. Sharon AI said it is deploying up to 68,000 Nvidia GPUs connected with Nvidia Quantum InfiniBand and Spectrum- X $TWTR Ethernet networking. Megaport is expanding access to Nvidia accelerated computing through its wholly owned subsidiary, Latitude.sh.
Nvidia said expanded access to its accelerated computing and Nemotron open models will allow organizations including healthcare startup Heidi and software company Atlassian $TEAM to build AI models, applications, and agents for local industries.
Nvidia and two of the partners named in Thursday's announcement, Sharon AI and Firmus, have a prior relationship. The two companies were initially named as partners in Nvidia 's AI Compute Partnership , a financing program under which Nvidia provided credit backing to cloud providers in return for a share of their revenue. Nvidia stepped away from that program last week after employees raised concerns about antitrust exposure, though the company left open the possibility of restructuring the initiative.
Nvidia 's equity investments in AI companies have grown sharply in 2026. The company's AI-related equity holdings reached $99 billion as of late July , up from approximately $7 billion a year earlier, as the chip company has moved to expand its position across the AI sector.

title: DOJ reportedly probes Nvidia-Groq deal for antitrust concerns
text:
DOJ reportedly probes Nvidia-Groq deal for antitrust concerns
Nvidia-Groq agreement raises questions about whether the AI chip companies are using the licensing and hiring deal to avoid antitrust review.
The Department of Justice is investigating whether Nvidia structured its arrangement with AI chip startup Groq to avoid antitrust scrutiny, according to two people with knowledge of the inquiry cited by The New York Times .
According to The New York Times , the DOJ opened the investigation shortly after Nvidia and Groq announced their deal in December and has since sent Nvidia a formal demand for information. Reuters independently reported the investigation, citing the Times account.
The DOJ hasn't confirmed the investigation. The department declined to comment on matters before the agency under its longstanding policy.
For IT infrastructure buyers and data center operators, the inquiry could affect how AI accelerator vendors structure technology partnerships and talent deals. It could also affect the competitive choices available to customers. Nvidia obtained Groq's inference technology and hired key personnel without acquiring the company, creating a transaction structure that could become more consequential if regulators determine it amounted to an acquisition in practice.
Nvidia paid billions for Groq technology
Nvidia disclosed the financial and accounting details in regulatory filings. It said it didn't purchase Groq's customer contracts, existing products or equity interests. Nvidia reported $13 billion in cash consideration at closing, with another $4 billion payable within a year.
Nvidia also recorded a $2.5 billion developed-technology intangible asset related to the arrangement.
The company has since incorporated Groq technology into its product portfolio. Nvidia introduced the Groq 3 LPX as an accelerator for its Vera Rubin platform , targeting low latency and large context AI workloads.
The issue it raises is whether this is in some sense an acquisition in sheep's clothing.
David Pearl Partner at Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer
When the agreement was announced, Groq said it would remain independent under then-CEO Simon Edwards and continue operating its cloud business.
The combination of a technology license with the hiring of Groq's top executives raises the question of whether the arrangement effectively functioned as an acquisition, said David Pearl, a partner at law firm Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer, who analyzed the Nvidia-Groq transaction.
"The issue it raises is whether this is in some sense an acquisition in sheep's clothing," Pearl said.
The question for regulators, he said, is whether Nvidia structured the deal as a license and hiring arrangement because the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976 doesn't cover those transactions , letting Nvidia avoid antitrust scrutiny, or whether the structure had legitimate business reasons.
Pearl said the DOJ's reported interest would be consistent with increased scrutiny of large technology companies, AI and compliance with the procedural requirements of the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act.
Senators questioned the deal months before reported DOJ probe
The reported investigation follows congressional scrutiny of the arrangement. Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., questioned Nvidia about the transaction in March, asking whether its structure was intended to avoid antitrust scrutiny.
The senators focused on Nvidia's combination of a technology license with the hiring of Groq's top executives and other employees. They argued that the arrangement could let Nvidia obtain important competitive assets without acquiring Groq as a company.
Warren, Blumenthal and Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., had separately urged the DOJ and Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to examine similar "reverse acquihire" arrangements involving major technology companies. Such transactions can combine technology and talent without the formal corporate acquisition that would ordinarily trigger merger review, the lawmakers said.
Groq has continued to operate independently since the Nvidia agreement. The company raised $650 million in June to expand its AI inference cloud and said it was targeting about 200 megawatts of capacity by the end of 2027.
Whether Groq continues operating as a genuinely independent company could become important to the DOJ's analysis, Pearl said. Regulators could look at factors including whether Groq retains customers and develops new products.
"Even if Groq remains technically independent, if the reality is that it exists now only to serve Nvidia, I suspect DOJ would view that as evidence that the transaction was a de facto acquisition," Pearl said.
If the DOJ ultimately has concerns about the transaction, a court challenge might not be the most likely outcome, Pearl said. The legal issues surrounding transactions structured to avoid a Hart-Scott-Rodino review remain relatively unsettled. Instead, the agencies could seek an agreement requiring Nvidia to notify the DOJ and FTC about future acquihire-like transactions for a period of several years, he said.
Such a settlement would address regulators' concerns about similar transactions without requiring the DOJ to establish a broader legal precedent in court.
TechTarget has contacted Nvidia and Groq for comment and will update this story if they respond.

title: Nvidia CEO Signals Strong Momentum for Shareholders
text:
After the market closed on Aug. 26, Nvidia ( NVDA +2.55% ) delivered its earnings report for the second quarter of its 2027 fiscal year -- a period that ended July 26. The company delivered another blowout quarter, with non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share of $2.22 on sales of $96.22 billion breezing past the average Wall Street analyst target of $2.10 per share on sales of $92.17 billion.
As impressive as the artificial intelligence (AI) hardware leader's fiscal Q2 report was, forward guidance and overall business commentary from the company's CEO, Jensen Huang, were arguably even more encouraging.
Jensen Huang outlined an incredible operating outlook for Nvidia
While Nvidia's year-over-year revenue growth of 106% in fiscal Q2 put the company's sales significantly above the average Wall Street guidance, its target for sales growth in the next fiscal year was even more surprising. While the average analyst estimate had modeled sales growth of 44% in fiscal 2028, Huang said that the company actually expected sales growth to come in at roughly 70%.
Meanwhile, the CEO said he anticipates gross margins to be between 72% and 73% for the year -- reflecting expectations that gross margins will improve after bottoming out at 71%-72% in the fourth quarter of the current fiscal year. For a heavily hardware-focused business, the idea of gross margins "bottoming" in the low-70s is incredible -- and it shows just how strong Nvidia's pricing power has remained. Notably, Huang also said the company's forecast of 70% annual sales growth next year reflected supply-constraint headwinds.
During the Q2 investor conference call, Huang also provided a very encouraging update on the scaling of Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform. Huang expects the Vera Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs) to have the fastest product ramp in the company's history, and Nvidia's opportunities in the AI compute stack are also rapidly expanding in other categories. While the company estimates a $25 billion revenue opportunity per gigawatt of AI compute with its Blackwell family of processors, it anticipates a $40 billion revenue opportunity per gigawatt with its Vera Rubin family.
Along with its leading position in AI GPUs, the company also sees huge expansion opportunities with its Vera central processing units (CPUs) and accompanying networking technologies. Huang expects CPU revenue to more than double next fiscal year, making Nvidia one of the leading suppliers in the server CPU market.
Commentary from the CEO and other leaders at the company suggests that the AI hardware leader is not only continuing to dominate the artificial GPU market across virtually all categories, but it's also scoring wins in other compute areas that should help it continue posting impressive sales and earnings growth.

title: Michael Burry Is Staying Short Nvidia, Palantir, and Tesla, Warning of a Possible "1987-Type Fall" for AI Stocks. Should Investors Take the Bet Seriously?
text:
Michael Burry Is Staying Short Nvidia, Palantir, and Tesla, Warning of a Possible "1987-Type Fall" for AI Stocks. Should Investors Take the Bet Seriously?
Michael Burry, famous for his depiction in The Big Short , has set his eyes on artificial intelligence ( AI) stocks . He's short Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Palantir (NASDAQ: PLTR), and Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) and sees the AI bubble leading to a "1987-type fall."
Leverage is a concern for people who need money soon
Burry noted that a rising stock market forces certain funds to go deeper into leverage. For instance, the GraniteShares 2x Long NVDA Daily ETF (NASDAQ: NVDL) is forced to buy more shares of Nvidia as the chipmaker rallies.
It's not just these funds, either. Margin investing is hot, and the total margin debt increased by 50% year over year in June. That type of leverage accelerates rallies but can lead to harsh, sudden crashes.
The risk of that level of margin was put on full display when Leopold Aschenbrenner's highly leveraged Situation Awareness hedge fund was liquidated due to declining stock prices. The fund had high-leverage bets on hot AI stocks. While most investors with long-term horizons can recover from a 20% dip, those same dips are devastating for investors like Aschenbrenner.
In the end, his $45 billion hedge fund liquidated almost overnight, catching the entire world by surprise and explaining why AI stocks had been slumping for weeks.
Even if you do not use leverage on AI stocks, you may still be affected by other people's leverage, since margin calls can force people to sell out of positions and turn small corrections into big ones.
Long-term investors shouldn't be worried
The AI boom is fueled by real demand, revenue, and profits. People are adopting AI models like ChatGPT and Gemini. Chatbots are becoming more common, and physical AI, such as humanoid robots and autonomous vehicles, is gaining traction.
It's not like the dot-com bubble, where companies had sketchy fundamentals and questionable long-term growth prospects. Furthermore, the margin unwind connected to Situational Awareness suggests there won't be a dramatic 1987-style event. There may be a good buying opportunity for patient investors.
Although Burry made a great call leading up to the recession that catapulted him to fame, he has repeatedly warned investors about stock market crashes that have never materialized.
Burry may have profited in the short run with some of his positions since he often uses puts. However, staying out of the market and avoiding growth stocks has hurt people in the long run.
Burry isn't right all the time, and when he makes bold bets, he's often thinking in months rather than years, since put options have expiration dates. It may also be the case that a broken clock is right twice a day. Burry disclosed a short position in Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS) on Aug. 6. The neocloud then delivered superb earnings and is up roughly 20% since that disclosure.
The market's love of leverage is a risk that can affect the entire market, with an outsized impact on growth stocks. However, the fundamental story for AI is solid and strengthening.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again
Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It's a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast.

title: Nvidia Rival Enflame Soars 206% in Shanghai Debut
text:
Nvidia Corp. ( NVDA , Financials ), the AI-chip leader whose products dominate high-end computing , now faces another well-funded challenger in China.
Enflame Technology surged 206% in its Shanghai trading debut Friday as investors rushed into another domestic alternative to Nvidia.
Retail demand exceeded the available shares by more than 6,000 times. That kind of opening creates a much bigger test.
Enflame reported 2025 revenue of 990 million yuan, or about $147 million, up from 722 million yuan a year earlier. The company has yet to turn a profit.
It intends to use the proceeds to develop fifth- and sixth-generation chips to compete with high-end international products. It's the right time.
Chinese chip suppliers have seen demand soar, helped by U.S. export restrictions and Beijing's drive for semiconductor self-sufficiency. Semiconductor capex in China will rise to $82 billion by 2030, Goldman Sachs estimates.
Other domestic chipmakers also saw huge gains on the first day, highlighting how aggressively investors are betting on China's AI hardware industry.
The 206% boom is just the beginning for investors. Next question: can Enflame translate policy support and strong demand into revenue growth fast enough to justify the valuation investors put on the company on day one.

title: I was an Nvidia DLSS 5 hater…until I used it myself
text:
Samples of DLSS 5 applied to games like NBA 2K27 and Resident Evil Requiem have raised concerns the graphical tech is basically a demanding AI algorithm that can "yassify" the look of games and interfere with the intent of game artists. But after trying it myself, I'm not so sure it's that big a deal...or that I have the willpower to stop using it.
I don’t know about you, but I was pretty leery of Nvidia’s new DLSS 5 tech when we first started seeing samples of how it can change the appearance of games in real time. I didn’t like the idea of Nvidia algorithmically injecting new details into my games that change the way they look, and I was afraid of the “yassifying” effect—that uncanny beautification you see in AI slop—we saw it apply in titles like Resident Evil Requiem .
…Then I tried it for myself this week. Now, I’m afraid I may be a reluctant believer.
Because while DLSS 5 is only officially supported in NBA 2K27 right now, entrepid modders have already ripped the DLSS files out of the game and made it fairly easy for anyone with an Nvidia GPU to start applying the new tech to whatever game(s) you like. And after throwing DLSS 5 on in the middle of my Star Wars Zero Company campaign, I’m not sure I’m ever going back.
Sure, going from DLSS 4 to DLSS 5 while playing Zero Company caused my framerate to drop off a cliff. But with Nvidia’s Frame Generation tech I was able to claw some of those frames per second back, and since Bit Reactor’s new Star Wars game is a turn-based tactics smorgasbord I’m not stressed about how heavy DLSS use might affect render quality or input latency. I just want my team of soldiers and scoundrels to look like they just stepped off a Volume set after a day of filming, and I’ll be damned if DLSS 5 doesn’t do exactly that.
Now look, I don’t exactly have a keen eye for fine details or framerates—I turn to an authority like Digital Foundry for that. Perhaps if I was more sensitive to those sorts of details my stomach would turn at how Nvidia’s burgeoning AI-powered image enhancement tech is changing the look of my game.
But to my eyes, going from DLSS 4 to DLSS 5 just made everything (and everyone) in my Zero Company game look a little bit better. Objects appear more elaborate and intricate, while faces look sharper and more detailed. Admittedly I do occasionally see textures take awhile to pop in, and now there’s a massive slowdown every time I enter a scene where DLSS is not running (typically just when I come back from missions and reload into the Den), but overall I feel like the game looks better (albeit runs worse) when DLSS 5 is switched on.
To show you what I mean, here’s a quick screenshot I captured of a Zero Company character under the effects of DLSS 5. While it’s not a perfect comparison, I think you can see the small changes in the way the character’s lips, chin and other facial features appear to be “yassified” compared to the original.
And this is just the beginning. If Nvidia puts in the work to fine-tune DLSS 5 and smooth out some of the performance issues over the coming months, it’s not hard for me to imagine this tech being treated like the next big step up for graphics in games. The fact that it’s basically just an AI filter being applied to your game after it’s rendered won’t matter to most people; what matters is that you can hit a button and make everyone in your game look a little more attractive.
But for me, the most exciting aspect of enabling DLSS 5 wasn’t the AI-fueled visual overhaul—it was figuring out how to get the tech running in Zero Company , then playing around with settings and sliders to see what it did to the game. It reminded me of that feeling I get when I upgrade the GPU in my gaming rig and start firing up old games (hello, Crysis and Cyberpunk ) to see how they look with the new card. In that way, it sort of feels like just another PC gaming upgrade you can choose to adopt, abandon, or adapt to your tastes.
With that perspective it’s easier to see DLSS 5 not as a shot across the bow of artistic intent in game development, but rather as one more tool that performance-minded PC enthusiasts can play with to fine-tune the look and feel of their favorite games. However, that only applies if players have the option to mess around with DLSS 5 settings…and the problem is that I suspect Nvidia won’t expose a lot of the controls I’ve been futzing around with to the average player.
See, in order to mod Zero Company to play well with DLSS 5 I had to use some third-party programs that let me enable the new graphical tech and mess around with how and when it modifies game graphics. But when DLSS 5 support officially appears in games like NBA 2K27 , it seems like you don’t have a lot of options for influencing how it affects the look of your game…just the choice to turn it on or off, as developers tune it for their specific artistic vision.
If that remains true for DLSS 5 in games going forward, then yes I think there’s still good reason to be leery of using it. It’s nice that Nvidia has committed to saying that game developers have full control over if and how DLSS 5 is implemented in their games, but I’m not sure I’d be comfortable using it unless I as a player had some control as well. Otherwise, it really does just feel like an AI is telling me what it thinks my character should look like, and that’s a bummer.
But after having so much fun modding my game and playing around with DLSS 5 settings this week, my eyes have been opened to the potential upsides of using this graphical enhancement tech. I think I was wrong to turn my nose up so quickly , and I’m excited to start messing around with it in more games. I just hope that when official DLSS 5 support starts rolling out for more titles, we see players given more control over how (not just if) it’s used.
This week your regular cohosts Adam Patrick Murray and Alaina Yee were joined by departing intern Glenn Mah and yours truly to dig into the launch of DLSS 5 and the rumors that Intel is gearing up to launch a monster 52-core CPU.
Later in the show longtime PCWorld model Mona joined us to take your questions from the chat as well as the Full Nerd Discord server. It was a lot of fun, and make sure you stick around to the end to hear all about how the show is changing now that Adam is leaving the Bay Area for beautiful North Carolina.
Don’t worry, the show will go on—and we’re going to have a new format to play around with!
Tired of hearing about DLSS? No worries, there’s a smorgasbord of other intriguing tech news out there this week!
Intel reportedly set to hike CPU prices by 10% ahead of ‘major annual product’ launch in March 2027 : The bad news keeps coming, as a recent report citing sources in the supply chain claims that we can expect Intel CPU prices to climb a bit this year. Hopefully these price hikes are more targeted at enterprise and server-grade CPUs rather than desktop chips, but we’ll see!

Nvidia’s free tool turns your idle home computers into a personal AI hub : I’m awfully leery of AI, but this new app from Nvidia might be interesting because it lets you run AI agents locally on your home network using the resources of whatever PCs you have. It supports not just Windows PCs but also Macs and Linux machines, which is pretty neat.
Top chipmakers embrace ASML’s $400M machines, agree to crucial chipmaking change : I’m still wrapping my head around this, but it sounds like TSMC and Samsung are signing on to use extreme ultraviolet lithography machines from Dutch firm ASML (Advanced Semiconductor Materials Lithography) that use lasers to create smaller features in next-gen chips.

title: Nvidia Is Letting Rival AI Chips Into Its Racks. Astera Labs Could Be the Quiet Winner
text:
NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) is doing something that initially sounds counterintuitive: making it easier for competing AI accelerators to live inside Nvidia-designed systems.
Reuters reported September 10 that inference-chip startup d-Matrix will use Nvidia's NVLink Fusion technology to connect its next-generation Raptor processors directly into Nvidia data-center racks. The systems are expected to become available in 2027. Astera Labs, Inc. (NASDAQ: ALAB ) is working with d-Matrix on custom connectivity solutions to move data rapidly across the system.
This creates an unusual three-layer architecture. d-Matrix supplies the accelerator, Nvidia supplies the rack-scale interconnect technology and architecture, and Astera helps solve the increasingly difficult problem of moving data between components.
Nvidia Can Win Without Selling Every Accelerator
For NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA), the bull case is that NVLink can become more valuable even when Nvidia does not sell every accelerator. If competing XPUs plug into Nvidia's rack architecture, Nvidia can shift from merely dominating GPUs to controlling an important system standard. That resembles the economics of owning the highway rather than insisting every vehicle on it be manufactured by the same company.
The bear case is obvious: NVLink Fusion deliberately makes alternative accelerators easier to deploy. If inference workloads become more heterogeneous, Nvidia could sacrifice some GPU unit share even while preserving influence over the broader system.
For Astera Labs, Inc. (NASDAQ:ALAB), heterogeneous systems may be an even cleaner opportunity. More accelerators, memory pools, CPUs and switches create more connectivity bottlenecks. Astera sells retimers, fabric switches and other connectivity products designed to address the data-movement challenges created by increasingly complex AI racks. The bearish argument is that ALAB's valuation already assumes substantial AI infrastructure growth and leaves little room for design delays or hyperscaler concentration.
Hedge-fund positioning became significantly more bullish on Astera Labs during Q2. Insider Monkey tracked 73 hedge funds in the stock, up from just 53 in Q1. Nvidia also increased to 285 hedge funds from 275. Short interest tells a more cautious story for Astera: roughly 6.6% of its float was short on August 14, compared with only about 1.2% for Nvidia. ALAB short interest nevertheless fell from the previous reporting period.
That divergence makes sense. Nvidia is the established platform owner; Astera is the higher-beta bet on connectivity complexity. NVLink Fusion reduces Nvidia's need to win every accelerator socket, while ALAB benefits from the messier, more heterogeneous AI infrastructure that this strategy encourages. Of the two, Nvidia remains the lower-risk position, but Astera may have more upside if rack-scale connectivity becomes one of the next major AI bottlenecks.

title: Latham’s Own AI Servers Give Firm Best Options, Leaders Say
text:
Latham & Watkins has purchased powerful computing chips from Nvidia that it is using to fine-tune open-weight models and provide an extra layer of security as it pursues an artificial intelligence strategy that isn’t limited to off-the-shelf tools.
Multiple leaders of Latham’s AI strategy committee told Bloomberg Law the firm decided to develop its own Nvidia server infrastructure three years ago and has been purchasing the servers over that same time period.
The servers are now active in a third-party data center facility that only Latham employees can access. The firm has purchased “multiple” H200 GPUs and is “actively looking” at adding Nvidia’s newer generation systems known as Blackwell and Vera Rubin, a spokesperson said.
Latham is experimenting with “fine-tuning” open-weight models developed by Nvidia , the Latham leaders said.
“The ability to integrate open-source models with our own software in an ‘on-prem’ basis and then run those tools in an integrated way puts us in a class that other law firms can’t match,” said Michael Rubin, global chair of Latham’s artificial intelligence practice who chairs the firm’s internal AI strategy committee.
The firm declined to disclose the cost of the endeavor.
Latham’s competitive argument goes further than data security. The Nvidia chips help the firm integrate its other internal systems with AI capabilities, said Rene Mendoza, Latham’s chief information officer. And lawyers on the AI committee say the investment helps them build unique tools that deliver their years of expertise in new ways.
The firm says its roster of technology employees has grown to 900, with about 100 of those specifically dedicated to AI.
“No AI company, no technology company will ever be able to replicate what we’re doing because they don’t have our lawyers,” said Amber Banks, an M&A and private equity partner and member of Latham’s AI strategy committee.
The unveiling of Latham’s Nvidia chips comes as firms are in a race to deploy artificial intelligence even as its impact on their business model remains unclear. Firms are using tools provided by legal AI firms including Harvey and Legora while frontier AI developers OpenAI and Anthropic have taken aim at building their own legal-specific tools.
Latham uses all those tools and has attorney-client relationships with many of the companies that develop them.
“Nobody can predict where any of this is going, so we have the best optionality,” Mendoza said.
Latham likely isn’t alone in pursuing private AI hardware.
Kirkland & Ellis, which Bloomberg Law reported in May has committed $500 million to build its own AI platform, posted job listings seeking AI infrastructure directors to develop and manage what the listings describe as “on‑premise Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) clusters.”
The language suggests Kirkland may already own AI hardware. Kirkland has declined on multiple occasions to comment on whether it has purchased GPU servers. The firm did not respond to a request for comment for this article.
Latham has advised Harvey on legal matters, including the company’s latest $550 million funding round, which this week valued the company at $15.5 billion. Nvidia is also a major Latham client. The firm represented the company last month on a massive data center campus to be built in Ohio and leased by OpenAI.
The firm’s buildout of Nvidia servers is not intended to lessen its reliance on Harvey, Rubin said. Latham said saving on token costs “is a factor” in its use of open-weight models, though that is not driving its decisions.
“This provides us capabilities that Harvey simply doesn’t offer,” Rubin said. “They’re in the cloud and this is on premise.”
Daryl Lim, the H. Laddie Montague Jr. Chair in Law at Penn State Dickinson Law, said the investment makes sense for a firm of Latham’s size but warned the math only works if the firm puts the servers to use. Buying, maintaining, and securing the systems is expensive and requires significant technical staff, he said. “If Latham can keep them busy on valuable work, the investment may be justified,” Lim said. “If not, outside providers make better commercial sense because they can spread those costs across many customers.”
The servers alone won’t deliver lasting advantage, Lim added. The real payoff comes if Latham uses the infrastructure to make its own legal work product and processes more useful across the firm. “That is where the competitive advantage is likely to lie,” he said.
Latham has been investing in AI engineers, lawyers with engineering backgrounds, and “innovation lawyers” who are embedded in practice groups to help develop new tools. It still is hiring for a range of open positions, including “innovation attorneys” and “AI services attorneys,” who will help roll out AI-enabled legal services.
“We are looking for people who can blend legal expertise, familiarity with law firms and client familiarity, with technical ability,” said Adam Ziegler, Latham’s director of artificial intelligence—legal innovation.
Even as firms lay out possibly tens of millions of dollars building new AI capabilities, some clients are already demanding it lessen the cost of legal services. Clients argue that AI reduces the amount of human time spent on certain tasks, and those savings should be shared with them.
But Latham, like its broader Big Law peers , has not seen a reduction in the number of hours lawyers are billing, Rubin said.
“We are still in very early days with this technology, so to predict in any sort of routine way or deterministic way what is the savings AI will bring to any given matter is very challenging to near impossible,” he said.
Ron Friedmann, a legal industry consultant, said Latham’s decision is reasonable but the outcome far from certain. “Owning and operating your own hardware makes sense in a world of uncertainty,” he said. “Is there a guarantee they’ll get paid back? No, but there’s no guarantee with anything anyone is doing right now.”
Rubin said it was difficult to predict how the cost of AI would grow in the future. He characterized Latham’s investment in AI services as “fairly agnostic to cost.”
“What I do know about Latham is that we are never going to stop investing in and making sure that we have the absolute best technology in front of our lawyers so they can do what they need to do to deliver the best client service,” he said.

title: Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia Top the List of Largest Companies by Market Cap. Here's the One I'm Buying Now.
text:
At the time of this writing, the three largest companies in the world are Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) at a $5.4 trillion market cap, Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) at $4.6 trillion, and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) at $4 trillion. There's still a decent gap between Alphabet and fourth-place Microsoft at $3.65 trillion, and an even larger gap to fifth-place Amazon at $2.7 trillion. But of the three largest companies in the world, which one makes the most sense to buy now?
I think there's a pretty clear-cut answer, as one stands out above the rest as a buy. But there's also an obvious stock in the top three that I think investors should avoid.
Two of these stocks have clear upside in the near future
Nvidia has risen to the position of the world's largest company thanks to huge demand for its GPU computing units. Artificial Intelligence (AI) demand appears insatiable, with little chance of a letdown. The AI hyperscalers are spending hundreds of billions right now, and Nvidia estimates that the big five will spend nearly $800 billion on data center capital expenditures this year alone. Next year, that figure is projected to rise to $1.3 trillion. That's enough demand for Nvidia to guide for 70% revenue growth next year, easily making it one of the fastest-growing companies in the world, let alone among the top three.
Alphabet is one of those big spenders, and estimates it will spend around $200 billion on data center capital expenditures this year. However, all of that spending is paying off. Alphabet is seeing huge success from its AI platform and is also seamlessly integrating AI overviews into Google Search to maintain its place as the top internet search tool in the world. Alphabet is also running a thriving cloud computing business in Google Cloud. This division is a direct beneficiary of increased computing capacity, and its revenue skyrocketed 82% last quarter. I think the growth case for Alphabet and Nvidia is far greater than Apple's; however, the market isn't valuing the stocks like that.

title: Desktop graphics card shipments hit four-year high of 12.5 million despite increasing prices — Nvidia takes 90% share as gamers rush to beat looming price spikes

Desktop graphics card shipments hit four-year high of 12.5 million despite increasing prices — Nvidia takes 90% share as gamers rush to beat looming price spikes | Tom's Hardware
Desktop graphics card shipments hit four-year high of 12.5 million despite increasing prices — Nvidia takes 90% share as gamers rush to beat looming price spikes
By Anton Shilov
Nvidia remains dominant supplier with a 90% market share.
Discrete graphics card shipments for desktop PCs in Q2 2026 totaled 12.5 million units, the highest number since Q1 2022 despite record-high prices and cratering shipments of desktop CPUs, according to findings from Jon Peddie Research . The result highlights a broader trend that shows that unit sales of standalone GPUs for gaming have so far remained immune to rising prices , perhaps because gamers are expecting even higher prices in the coming quarters.
The industry shipped 12.5 million standalone graphics cards for desktop PCs in the second quarter of 2026, up around 5.9% sequentially and 7.8% year-over-year. 12.5 million add-in boards (AIBs) is the highest number of graphics cards sold in one quarter since the first quarter of 2022, when the industry shipped 13.38 million AIBs.
It is particularly noteworthy that 2026 is shaping up to be better for unit sales of desktop graphics boards than 2025 despite raising prices. For the first half of 2026, 24.3 million desktop AIBs were shipped, up significantly from 20.8 million graphics cards supplied in the first half of 2026. JPR analysts also note that only around 14 million desktop PCs were sold during the quarter, which — given an unusually high 89% attach rate — largely means that the majority of AIBs shipped during the quarter were aimed at gamers buying in retail and not at PC makers.
"Defying common wisdom, high-end AIB sales spiked as prices increased," said Jon Peddie, president of JPR. "Our theory is consumers rushed to buy AIBs before the prices went any higher, as the war in Iran is driving prices up in all segments."
Having shipped about 11.25 million discrete GPUs for desktop computers in Q2 2026, Nvidia remained the undisputed leader of the market with around 90% market share. AMD controlled roughly 8% of the market, shipping about one million discrete desktop GPUs, while Intel's share increased to 2% on shipments of several hundred thousand units. Meanwhile, Jon Peddie Research notes that market share changes were negligible during the quarter: AMD’s overall AIB market share decreased by -0.16% from the previous quarter, Intel's market share increased by 0.3%, and Nvidia's market share decreased by -0.1%.
For Nvidia, the quarter was particularly good as it sold the highest quantity of discrete GPUs for desktop PCs in a single quarter since Q3 2017, when it sold approximately 11.72 million units. By contrast, sales of AMD's standalone graphics cards have been floating below or around one million units per quarter for nearly four years now, with only three quarters being exceptions (Q3 2023, Q4 2023, Q4 2024). Still, one million is higher than the around 700 thousand discrete desktop GPUs the company sold in Q2 2025.
In total, Nvidia shipped approximately 17.365 million discrete graphics processors in the second quarter: roughly 11.25 million units went to desktops, and around 6.115 million units were installed into notebook and compact PCs. Since both AMD and Intel have quietly quit the market for standalone GPUs for mobile PCs, their shipments to this market segment were essentially zero.

Agentic LLM systems have moved from linear prompt chains to graph-based workflows and, more recently, code-executing harnesses. The article advises validating model outputs and choosing the least complex design that meets reliability, speed, and cost needs.

By treating agents as distributed systems, he discusses state ownership, message passing, write-through state, and supervision boundaries to manage failures, continuations, and mutable execution graphs, moving agentic workflows beyond fragile demos to resilient architecture.

Work through your production AI decisions with senior engineers from other companies. Apply their perspectives to challenges from your own work.
Building RAG pipelines or AI agents? Work through retrieval, context, evals, and reliability decisions with experienced practitioners.
NVIDIA Personal AI Router (PAIR), now available in beta, lets you combine the inference capacity of multiple computers on your local network and automatically distribute AI requests among them . It is primarily designed for local multi-agent AI workloads, where multiple independent model calls could otherwise overwhelm a single GPU.
NVIDIA says a breadth-first approach to distributing agentic tasks is becoming increasingly common, with a lead agent dispatching subtasks to sub-agents or multiple agents working together to complete more complex tasks. However, this approach can create a bottleneck on the local GPU when it receives too many requests.
To address this challenge, NVIDIA PAIR maximizes the AI compute available locally by distributing individual inference requests across available systems. It integrates seamlessly with popular local inference services such as Ollama and LM Studio without requiring changes to the underlying architecture or agent harness.
Agents can send a request through the familiar local interface it expects. PAIR receives the request through its proxy, identifies its engine and model requirements, and selects one eligible node. That node executes the request from start to finish and sends the response back through PAIR. The agent continues to see one connection while PAIR handles placement behind it.
To demonstrate PAIR’s capabilities, NVIDIA released a demo combining Hermes Desktop, Ollama, and PAIR showing roughly a 2x reduction in completion time when combining an RTX Spark, a DGX Spark, and an RTX 5090 via PAIR compared with running the workload on a single RTX Spark laptop. In the demo, Hermes breaks the task into five independent specialist analyses, delegates them, reconciles their findings, and synthesizes the final plan—covering what needs to happen tonight, this week, later, or not at all. PAIR handles the distribution of these inference requests across available nodes, while Ollama runs the model on whichever node PAIR selects. NVIDIA notes, however, that the demo should not be taken as a performance guarantee, as results depend on multiple factors including workload parallelism, model, engine settings, hardware, network, and node availability.
NVIDIA PAIR can be used on Windows 11, Linux, and macOS, with support for both x64 and arm64 systems. It can also pair nodes running different operating systems, dispatching a task to a given node only if the required model or engine is known to be compatible with that node. NVIDIA explicitly notes that PAIR does not "merge GPUs or pool VRAM into one larger accelerator". Instead, it distributes individual inference requests across available systems.
Despite these disclaimers, NVIDIA's announcement sparked some confusion on social media, with users interpreting PAIR as a solution for sharing their available compute with third parties or for running complex models by combining less capable compute .
Reddit user Vegetable-Warthog81 described their positive experience with PAIR , using it to distribute inference across three RTX 5090s running Qwen 3.8 27B using Ollama:
PAIR makes distributing jobs across the three machines pretty painless. For long, repetitive “grunt work” where I care more about stability and just keeping all the GPUs busy than squeezing out maximum tokens/sec, it’s been surprisingly nice.
PAIR can be downloaded from GitHub. For a step-by-step introduction to using it, see the Getting Started documentation.

title: Kalshi wants 24/7 Tesla and Nvidia perps as Wall Street fights over who regulates them
text:
Kalshi wants 24/7 Tesla and Nvidia perps as Wall Street fights over who regulates them
The prediction-market operator plans to seek U.S. approval for about 60 stock and ETF perps, taking one of crypto's biggest trading products into equities.
Kalshi plans to seek regulatory approval for about 60 perpetual futures tied to stocks and exchange-traded funds, including Tesla, Apple and Nvidia, that could trade around the clock.
If approved, the contracts would be the first regulated single-stock perpetual futures in the United States, allowing leveraged bets without expiration dates.
Citadel Securities warned that placing equity-linked perpetual futures outside Securities and Exchange Commission oversight could create a “parallel shadow market” with weaker safeguards against insider trading and market manipulation.
Prediction marketplace Kalshi is planning to bring one of crypto's most popular trades to U.S. stocks, with perpetual futures tied to companies including Tesla, Apple and Nvidia that could trade around the clock.
The operator plans to seek regulatory approval for roughly 60 perpetual futures linked to individual stocks and exchange-traded funds, the Wall Street Journal reported late Thursday . If approved, they would be the first regulated single-stock perps offered in the U.S.
Perpetual futures, usually called perps, let traders bet on whether an asset will rise or fall, often with borrowed money, without the contract ever expiring. Traders instead make regular payments to one another that help keep the contract near the price of the asset it tracks.
They have become one of crypto's largest businesses since the soon to be defunct exchange BitMEX introduced these products in 2016, with newer venues such as Hyperliquid letting traders take leveraged positions on bitcoin and hundreds of tokens at any hour.
A Tesla perp could keep trading through nights and weekends while Tesla shares on Nasdaq are closed, creating a live view of what traders think the company is worth hours, or even days, before the stock itself reopens.
But that has raised concerns among U.S. regulators. Is a perpetual contract tied to a stock a futures product overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, or does it belong with the Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulates the underlying shares?
Kalshi already won CFTC approval in May for a bitcoin perpetual contract. The regulator classified it as a futures contract, but warned the structure might not work for every asset class and said perps tied to other kinds of assets should go through individual review.
Not everyone is convinced, however.
Prominent trading firm Citadel Securities told the SEC and CFTC in a Thursday letter that products tied to U.S. public companies should remain under SEC oversight.
Moving them elsewhere could create a "parallel shadow market" disconnected from the surveillance used across U.S. stocks and options, the firm said.
The concern is easy to see with a company like Nvidia or Tesla. An employee with undisclosed earnings information could theoretically trade a perp while the stock market is shut. A company could also release major news during a trading halt while its perpetual contract keeps moving, unless the two markets coordinate.
Citadel said SEC oversight already connects trading across stocks, options and related products, helping regulators spot insider trading or attempts to move one market through another.
It further pointed to rules around trading halts, order handling and market access that may not automatically carry over if equity-linked perps trade under a different regime.
Crypto traders have spent years buying leveraged assets around the clock, and the question now is whether a product built for a market that never closes can be bolted onto one that does.
By CoinDesk Research

title: Nvidia's Huang Dismisses Circular Financing Worries, Touts $100 Billion Contract Backlog
text:
Nvidia's Huang Dismisses Circular Financing Worries, Touts $100 Billion Contract Backlog
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed concerns that the company is fueling its own demand through investments in AI labs and cloud providers, telling a Goldman Sachs conference that if the strategy is circular, "let's do more of that." He said Nvidia has roughly $100 billion of contracted customer demand behind the projects it helps finance and that the company deploys minimal capital relative to the business generated. The comments pushed back against skeptics including Michael Burry and Jim Chanos, who have raised alarms about circular spending and GPU depreciation. Nvidia disclosed $99 billion in equity investments as of July 26 and has guaranteed up to $105 billion for OpenAI's Ohio data center lease. The company's second-quarter revenue rose 106% year over year to $96.2 billion.
Jensen Huang has a blunt message for critics who argue Nvidia is propping up its own sales by financing the very companies that buy its chips: bring it on.
The chief executive of the world's most valuable semiconductor company used an appearance at Goldman Sachs' Communacopia + Technology Conference on Thursday to mock the "circular financing" narrative that has gained traction among short sellers and skeptics, including Michael Burry and Jim Chanos. His defense came as Nvidia's expanding role as both investor and lender across the AI ecosystem has drawn scrutiny from regulators and market participants alike.
"Is that circular? If that is, let's do more of that," Huang said when Goldman analyst Jim Schneider pressed him on the company's guarantees and financial backing for AI labs and cloud providers.
The exchange highlighted a central tension in the AI investment boom: how much of the demand for Nvidia's hardware is organic, and how much is being manufactured by Nvidia's own balance sheet?
The concerns are not difficult to understand. Nvidia invests in an AI startup or a cloud computing company. That company then uses the capital to buy Nvidia GPUs. The revenue flows back to Nvidia, and the cycle repeats. The distinction between a genuine sale and a self-funded one becomes blurry.
Nvidia's financial footprint across the AI stack has grown substantially. The company disclosed $99 billion of equity investments as of July 26, plus another $25 billion in future investment commitments. In January, it put $2 billion into CoreWeave, a cloud provider that rents out Nvidia GPUs and has borrowed billions against them. The company also agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion so OpenAI can lease a data center campus in Ohio that will run on Nvidia chips. Nvidia pays nothing unless OpenAI defaults, but its total guarantees could reach $108.5 billion.
On August 10, Nvidia expanded its role further by partnering with six financial institutions—Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR—on platforms aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion of third-party capital for AI infrastructure. That figure is a target for outside financing, not a direct Nvidia commitment. "Hopefully, most of that $500 billion is going to be asset-backed," Huang said on Thursday.
The equity ties run in several directions at once. In late February, OpenAI announced $110 billion of new investment at a $730 billion pre-money valuation, including $30 billion each from Nvidia and SoftBank Group and $50 billion from Amazon. Huang said that same month that an earlier, widely discussed plan for Nvidia to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI "was never a commitment." For SoftBank, the bet has meant reshuffling its own portfolio: the Japanese group sold its entire $5.83 billion Nvidia stake in October 2025 to help fund its OpenAI investment, and it has been paying in its $30 billion commitment in $10 billion tranches, the second of which was funded by a bridge loan.
Huang's counterargument is straightforward: the capital Nvidia deploys is small relative to the business it generates. "We put in one and 100 comes back in," he said.
He also claimed the company has unusually strong visibility into the projects it supports. "We brought the pipeline to them," Huang said. "I'm not taking any risks. I need a sure thing."
Behind those projects, Huang said, sits roughly $100 billion of contracted customer demand. "It's lined-up contracts. It's total contracted value. It's real stuff."
The strategy, he argued, is necessary to build a global network of newer cloud providers that can serve as "distribution channels for NVIDIA's architecture."
The counterargument has been building for months. Short seller Jim Chanos challenged Huang directly this week after the CEO posted GPU rental data on X, formerly Twitter. When Huang called Nvidia compute "durable and highly rentable," Chanos replied: "Then why not rent them out yourself?" He later said the jab was aimed at companies that buy Nvidia chips to rent them out, not at Nvidia itself.
Chanos has warned of a "depreciation time bomb" at companies such as CoreWeave and Oracle, arguing that chips can become economically obsolete within three to four years even while still running. He is short data-center and neocloud stocks.
Michael Burry, who correctly predicted the 2008 housing crash, first disclosed bearish put options on Nvidia through his Scion Asset Management in November 2025, before winding down the fund late that year. He now shares his trades on his Substack, Cassandra Unchained, where he said in an August 11 post that he had added to his Nvidia short. His argument centers on accounting: cloud companies are depreciating their GPU fleets too slowly, inflating reported profits. Google, Microsoft, and Oracle depreciate their servers over about six years. Burry contends two to three years is closer to the truth given how quickly Nvidia ships new architectures, and he estimated the cloud providers are understating depreciation costs by roughly $176 billion between 2026 and 2028.
Company filings show that the hyperscalers themselves do not agree on the answer. Most lengthened their schedules over the past four years, but Amazon went the other way: effective January 2025, it cut the useful life of a subset of its servers and networking equipment from six years to five, citing "the increased pace of technology development, particularly in the area of artificial intelligence and machine learning."

Note: Useful lives cover servers and network equipment as disclosed in company filings. Meta expected its extension to cut 2025 depreciation expense by about $2.9 billion; Amazon said its shorter schedule added $1.4 billion to 2025 depreciation and amortization.
Burry warned in July that circular spending had reached "biblical proportions," pointing to a jump in the cost of insuring Nvidia's debt. He has also argued that the new $500 billion financing platform recreates the kind of risky debt dynamics that fed the 2008 crisis.
Regulators have begun to take notice as well. The IMF noted in its April Global Financial Stability Report that a downturn could hit the value of firms along the AI value chain that have increasingly relied on circular financing, although it said the impact on financial stability appears modest for now. The Bank for International Settlements went further on September 10. In a speech in Mumbai, BIS General Manager Pablo Hernández de Cos said the AI investment boom is increasingly financed "not by earnings but through debt and, notably, through private credit," and warned that if returns to AI disappoint, a pullback in investment "could turn today's capital expenditure boom into a bust." He compared the risk to the British railway mania of the 1840s and the dotcom surge of the late 1990s, booms whose corrections had economy-wide implications. He also noted that upstream exporters in the AI supply chain, such as Taiwan, South Korea, Malaysia, and Singapore, have gained as prices for AI-related goods rose.
Nvidia's underlying business continues to surge, which lends weight to Huang's confidence. Second-quarter revenue jumped 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, while data center revenue rose 117% to $89 billion. Over the last 12 months, the company generated $303 billion in revenue with gross margins near 75%.
Huang reiterated his forecast that AI infrastructure spending could reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. He said Nvidia could grow revenue 70% year over year and noted that Grace Blackwell NVLink 72-rack systems recorded 27% month-over-month growth. He also said about $400 billion of venture capital had flowed into "AI native" companies—which he defined as those spending two-thirds of the money they raise on compute—over the past six months.

Huang also pointed to system pricing trends as evidence of sustained demand. Hopper systems sold for about $18,000 per GPU, Blackwell for about $25,000, and the upcoming Vera Rubin architecture is expected to command roughly $40,000.
The GPU rental market has provided another data point. Huang shared data from Ornn Exchange showing rental prices for H100 chips jumped 22% in one month to $3.28 per hour. The H100 launched in 2022. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator said on the company's second-quarter earnings call that a batch of H100 GPUs coming off an expired contract was immediately rebooked at 95% of the original price. Silicon Data, which tracks GPU residual values, put the resale value of six-year-old A100 chips at around $5,000 as of September.
"All of the data points that I'm getting are telling me that the infrastructure retains value," Intrator said.
Huang made the same point in an August post on X, highlighting that CoreWeave signed a contract to rent A100 GPUs through 2029. The A100 launched in May 2020. "The mighty A100 fleet are mission-capable from 2020 through 2029," Huang wrote. "NVIDIA compute is fungible, durable, and highly rentable. It is a productive, revenue-generating asset."
Huang's own back-of-the-envelope math at the conference used the same six-year schedule that Burry disputes. A one-gigawatt data center, he said, costs "probably like $60 billion," or about $10 billion a year spread over six years, while such capacity currently generates about $50 billion a year in rental revenue.
Beyond the financing debate, Huang used the Goldman conference to outline Nvidia's expanding reach across the AI ecosystem. The company's platform runs models from major developers including OpenAI, Google's Gemini, Meta, Anthropic, and xAI. OEM partners include Dell, Super Micro, Lenovo, HP, and Cisco. Neocloud partners include CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda, and Firmus.
Huang said this broad reach reduces Nvidia's dependence on any single customer or sales channel. He likened Nvidia's position to that of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., arguing that capacity is among the contract chipmaker's most important values: "The way I see TSMC is the way that AI natives and AI companies see us." The company's SEC filings showed its three largest direct customers accounted for 16%, 15%, and 13% of revenue in the first half of fiscal 2027.
He identified cybersecurity and physical AI as major future opportunities, citing partnerships with CrowdStrike, Cisco, and Palantir in security, Mercedes and Uber in autonomous vehicles, and Amazon in warehouse and logistics systems. Nvidia is also working with Nokia on AI-RAN and 6G technology, which Huang described as a form of physical AI that effectively creates a distributed edge data center.
Constraints remain. Huang acknowledged upstream supply challenges in packaging, memory, connectors, voltage regulators, and wafers. Downstream, land, electricity, and ready-to-use data-center capacity are the bigger bottlenecks. He pointed to Australia as an example, where Nvidia is working with companies and data-center operators on plans involving 2 gigawatts of capacity for 2027, valued at about $80 billion.
Prediction-market traders remain bullish on the stock. Polymarket gives Nvidia a 79% chance of finishing 2026 as the world's largest company by market capitalization, versus about 13% for Apple and 6% for Alphabet.
The debate over circular financing is unlikely to be resolved by a single conference appearance. But Huang's willingness to engage directly with the bear case—and his insistence that the numbers speak for themselves—signals that Nvidia sees the criticism as a narrative problem, not a business one.

title: Nvidia Rebounds After Rivals Open a 10-Point Weekly Gap
text:
Nvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA ), the dominant artificial-intelligence accelerator supplier, climbed roughly 0.6% to $220.43 Friday, finding buyers after a bruising stretch against rival chipmakers. The shares had lost about 5% since Tuesday, Barron's reported, while AMD ( NASDAQ:AMD ) and Qualcomm ( NASDAQ:QCOM ) advanced around 5%a striking performance gap of nearly ten percentage points.
Amazon's major AI-chip agreement with Qualcomm gave investors another reason to explore alternatives to Nvidia. Yet the financial scoreboard remains brutally one-sided. Nvidia produced $89 billion in data-center revenue during its fiscal second quarter , a 117% surge representing roughly 92.5% of total sales. Management now expects third-quarter revenue of approximately $108 billion.

title: Google’s $15 Billion Finland AI Build Is Good News for Nvidia, With One Important Catch

title: China-modified Nvidia RTX 5090 with massive 96GB of memory appears on Alibaba for less than $4,000 — 3x more VRAM at 65% the cost of the original
text:
China-modified Nvidia RTX 5090 with massive 96GB of memory appears on Alibaba for less than $4,000 — 3x more VRAM at 65% the cost of the original
By Zhiye Liu
The GeForce RTX 5090 is already at the pinnacle of the best graphics cards . However, Shenzhen Suqiao Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd., a Chinese OEM/ODM, has reportedly made it even more powerful by outfitting the Blackwell flagship with 96GB of memory, 3X more than the original. The company is already selling these modified GeForce RTX 5090 96GB on Alibaba for $3888 , 35% less than the vanilla GeForce RTX 5090 in the U.S.
You can say whatever you want about China, but you cannot deny that factories there have produced some of the most interesting modified graphics cards, including the GeForce RTX 5080 32GB , the GeForce RTX 4090 48GB , and the GeForce RTX 3090 48GB. While some of these projects are fueled by pure curiosity, most of them are a result of the recent AI boom that has stimulated Chinese factories to think outside the box and give existing and even past graphics cards a memory upgrade so consumers can repurpose them for AI workloads. While we have seen a fair share of absurd rumors, such as the GeForce RTX 5090 128GB , the conjuration of the GeForce RTX 5090 96GB seems more plausible from a technical standpoint, and there is precedent for a Blackwell-based graphics card with 96GB of memory.
Before diving into the GeForce RTX 5090 96GB, it is worth noting that the Alibaba listing is from Suqiao, a Chinese manufacturer with over 10 years of experience making graphics cards, motherboards, and servers. So it is not a random Chinese chop shop but rather an established OEM/ODM, which lends some credence to the existence of the GeForce RTX 5090 96GB. Needless to say, the Alibaba listing is full of questionable specifications, such as GDDR6X memory or memory speeds of 14 Gbps.
The RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell , which has 96GB of GDDR7 memory, uses the same GB202 silicon as the GeForce RTX 5090, but with more enabled Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs). Therefore, a 96GB configuration is possible on GB202; however, the GeForce RTX 5090 96GB likely uses a custom PCB, allowing the manufacturer to install the memory chips in clamshell mode, which doubles the total memory on the PCB. The vendor could either procure the GB202 silicon individually or extract it from mainstream GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards and reball it onto the custom PCB.
Even in clamshell mode, with memory pads on both sides of the PCB, there are only 32 of them. The RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell has 32 GDDR7 chips, each 24Gb (3GB) in capacity. The problem we have with the GeForce RTX 5090 96GB that raises a red flag about its authenticity is the mention of GDDR6X. Micron only produced GDDR6X memory chips in 16 Gb (2GB), so the maximum capacity would be 48GB in clamshell mode. Plus, GDDR6X operates between 19 Gbps and 24 Gbps, much higher than the listed 14 Gbps, which corresponds to standard GDDR6.
Modified firmware and software-level hacks are necessary to run Nvidia graphics cards with modified memory capacity. For instance, the GeForce RTX 4090 48GB was possible because modders modified Nvidia's firmware to get these graphics cards running. However, rumors on the street suggest that a leaked firmware for the GeForce RTX 5090 has been available for a few months, which could explain why we are starting to see these GeForce RTX 5090 96GB graphics cards surface.
Suqiao listed the GeForce RTX 5090 96GB for $3,888, significantly lower than other Alibaba merchants who have it closer to $5,900. For reference, custom GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards start at $6,000 in the U.S. market. After the latest price hikes, Nvidia is selling the RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell for $16,000, although it can go up to $17,999 , depending on which variant you pick up. If the GeForce RTX 5090 96GB is real, even at $6,000, it would be a steal for anyone running AI models.
Still not enough VRAM for techtube.
Maybe the listing is fake, but this kind of modification shouldn't be too hard. It's just turning an RTX 5090 into a NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition with slightly fewer cores enabled.
Micron has a roadmap suggesting 4 GB (32 Gb) GDDR7 modules will come within a couple years.
So eventually, you will see 128 GB GDDR7 on a 512-bit GPU (32 modules in clamshell configuration).
I doubt we'll see consumer clamshell cards again. It's a terrible design compromise where you run your VRAM at half speed to get more capacity. Something workstation or datacenter GPUs do but not something a consumer needs.
The popular 9060 XT 16GB uses clamshell memory. It has the same 128-bit bus and memory bandwidth as a 9060 XT 8GB. I don't think anybody cares that the memory chips aren't technically being used to their full potential as they would be on a 256-bit memory bus, it's all about the capacity on a "budget" GPU. Doubled bandwidth could increase performance, but it would also increase power consumption of the card.
Same story with the 5060 Ti 16GB. There's usually at least one card like this per generation. Even the 64-bit 6500 XT 8GB, although not many of those got made.
I guess I could see the rise of 3 GB and 4 GB GDDR7 modules putting an end to clamshell cards, IF the prices are not super-inflated as 3 GB modules supposedly are right now.
If you can give the consumer 16 GB on 128-bit using 4x4GB, no clamshell, is there any point to giving them more (such as 8x3GB)? Probably not, unless the next-gen console games are extremely VRAM demanding.
I think JEDEC has specified 6 GB and 8 GB GDDR7 modules in the GDDR7 standard, but there's no guarantee that memory manufacturers will ever make them before moving onto the next thing.
The popular 9060 XT 16GB uses clamshell memory.
Yes and it's a bad design. Those DRAM chips have half their traces disconnected. If you are going to use eight GDDR DRAM chips then you need to use eight 32-bit memory channels for them.
Each GDDR DRAM chip is a 32-bit interface that accepts two 16-bit commands per cycle. You are halving your memory performance to double capacity, which is a bad trade off for consumers as performance is almost universally limited by memory bandwidth not capacity.
The only reason we even see that in consumer space is because the memory cartel was years behind on 24/32Gb modules and techtubers used rage bait to spread misinformation online.
Doubled bandwidth could increase performance, but it would also increase power consumption of the card.
That is not how power consumption works, clamshell mode use's more power because eight chips use more power then four. Halving the traces does not reduce their power usage, it's the same voltage and clock speed. If anything it's lower total memory performance as you spend twice as much power budget on those extra chips and need more VRAM cooling for it, though the monster is still the GPU itself.

title: China's AI chip IPO boom rolls on as another Nvidia challenger soars 200% in market debut
text:
By Huileng Tan
Enflame is among a new wave of Chinese AI chipmakers raising capital as Beijing pushes for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Investors are piling into China's artificial intelligence chipmakers as Beijing's push to build domestic alternatives to Nvidia fuels a new wave of blockbuster IPOs.
On Friday, Shanghai Enflame Technology surged about 200% in its debut on Shanghai's tech-focused Star market after raising 6.12 billion yuan, or $913 million.
Backed by the Chinese gaming giant Tencent, Enflame develops AI chips for training and inference, making it one of a new generation of domestic chipmakers benefiting from Beijing's push for semiconductor self-sufficiency amid US export restrictions.
Enflame's online retail tranche was more than 6,000 times oversubscribed, underscoring strong investor appetite for Chinese AI chipmakers.
Enflame's debut follows the December listing of fellow AI GPU designer Moore Threads, another Chinese startup seeking to challenge Nvidia, as well as the recent high-profile IPOs of memory chipmaker CXMT and robotics company Unitree.
The listing also offers a glimpse into the economics of China's emerging AI chipmakers.
In 2025, Enflame's revenue rose 37% to 990 million yuan, while its loss excluding non-recurring items narrowed to 1.20 billion yuan, according to the company's listing prospectus. Meanwhile, its largest customer, Chinese internet and gaming giant Tencent, accounted for nearly 84% of sales. The company expects to break even in 2026 or 2027.
Enflame's strong market debut reflects growing investor appetite for Chinese AI and semiconductor IPOs.
China is "still at a very early stage of a multi-year IPO upcycle" as semiconductor, AI infrastructure, and robotics companies tap public markets to fund research and expansion, wrote Morgan Stanley analysts in a note on August 28.
The bank said many of the new listings are developing technologies China sees as strategically important, with companies investing more heavily in research and capital spending, though many have yet to become profitable.
"Capital markets are therefore critical to help them scale up," the bank's analysts wrote.

title: Forget AMD. Here's Who Nvidia Really Needs to Be Worried About.
text:
The question of which AI hardware company is best seems to always circle around Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD +3.09% ) and Nvidia ( NVDA +2.55% ) . However, I don't think that's who Nvidia shareholders need to be concerned about.
Instead, I think investors need to look outside the GPU realm and start looking at custom AI chips that could steal market share. The biggest name in this space is Broadcom ( AVGO +2.83% ) , and I think it is actually Nvidia's No. 1 competitor right now.
This shifts the narrative completely, and once you see the growth Broadcom is projecting, it's easy to understand why Nvidia has cause for concern.
AMD's results aren't as impressive as Nvidia's
First, let's figure out why AMD isn't a threat. At the start of the AI arms race, Nvidia captured a lot of the data center computing market share because its products were flat-out better than AMD's. The biggest advantage Nvidia had was its CUDA software, which controls how its GPUs process calculations. AMD didn't have a great counterpart to this software, so every company naturally gravitated toward Nvidia's GPUs. While there could be some arguments made for whether AMD's or Nvidia's hardware is better today, the reality is that a vast majority of existing infrastructure is already set up for Nvidia GPUs , so a wholesale switch is highly unlikely due to switching costs.
Additionally, Nvidia is still growing faster despite AMD's smaller size (which should ideally make it easier to grow faster). During Nvidia's Q2, ended July, its data center division grew at a 117% pace to $89 billion. AMD's data center division generated a mere $6.7 billion and grew at a 107% pace. That clearly indicates Nvidia is still growing faster and has a huge size advantage as well.
However, another competitor is rising.
Broadcom forecasts monster growth over the next few years
GPU-based computing is great for all sorts of workloads, and the flexibility it provides is unparalleled. However, GPUs aren't always used for their full capabilities, and sometimes end up running one workload over their entire lifespan. That wastes many features, making it not optimized for the task.
As the AI build-out progresses, the AI hyperscalers are looking to optimize computing costs, and that means developing custom AI hardware specifically built for workloads they will see. There will always be a place for GPUs in AI, as there may be odd data sets or other workloads that aren't suited for custom AI chips, but a healthy amount of workloads can be run for cheaper on optimized hardware.
None of the AI hyperscalers has the expertise to design and build its own computing chip, so they bring on a partner like Broadcom to handle this. This creates a great relationship, as Broadcom brings the manufacturing capabilities and design knowledge, while the AI hyperscalers bring massive computing demand.
Broadcom has four major clients: Alphabet , Meta Platforms , OpenAI, and Anthropic. Currently, Alphabet's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) is the only computing unit being used in large numbers. Still, the other three are ramping up their orders, which is causing Broadcom's revenue to grow rapidly. During the fiscal third quarter (ended Aug. 2), Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue totaled $16.7 billion, up 221% year over year.
While that's smaller than Nvidia by a long shot, it's growing far faster than either Nvidia or AMD. Furthermore, Broadcom expects its AI semiconductor revenue to double in 2027 to $115 billion and again in 2028 to $230 billion. That makes it a force to be reckoned with in the computing space, and I think Nvidia has more to worry about with Broadcom than it does with AMD.
I think the best way to invest in AI computing is to take positions in both Nvidia and Broadcom, as I have done. That way, you can benefit from whichever one ends up being the winner . While I think both of these companies will end up sharing a large portion of market share, Broadcom is certainly growing faster right now and is well-positioned to continue capturing additional market share.

title: TSM’s Record Sales Say AI Chips Are Booming. The Nvidia-AMD Fight Is Now About Who Keeps the Margin

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMD ) are competing for AI accelerator share, but Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's latest sales show one thing both companies agree on: demand for advanced silicon remains enormous.
TSM reported September 10 that August revenue reached a record NT$514.81 billion, up 53.3% from a year earlier. Concerns that TSM could raise prices by as much as 10% next year nevertheless weighed on semiconductor shares.
That creates an interesting dynamic for Nvidia and AMD. Both companies benefit from rising AI-compute demand, but both depend on a manufacturing ecosystem whose suppliers are gaining bargaining power.
NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) has a bull case built around its platform advantage. CUDA, networking, NVLink and rack-scale systems make the company much harder to displace than a standalone chip vendor. Customers increasingly evaluate total system performance rather than raw accelerator specifications.
The bear case is cost. Foundry, HBM and advanced-packaging suppliers all want a larger portion of AI system economics. Nvidia has historically enjoyed extraordinary gross margins because demand exceeded supply and its software ecosystem was difficult to replicate. The more expensive the rest of the bill of materials becomes, the harder those margins become to defend.
AMD Needs Share Gains to Overwhelm the Cost Pressure
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) has a bull case built around hyperscalers desperately wanting competition. A credible alternative can win major deployments without overtaking Nvidia industry-wide. Each large customer also gives AMD more software feedback and improves the maturity of its ecosystem.
AMD's bearish problem is that it may have less ability than Nvidia to pass higher manufacturing costs through to customers. A challenger often needs aggressive pricing precisely when input costs are moving against it.
Hedge-fund sentiment became more bullish on both stocks in Q2. Nvidia ownership rose to 285 funds from 275, while AMD surged to 164 from 134. Short interest remained modest, although it was higher for AMD: approximately 2.5% of AMD's float was short as of August 14 versus roughly 1.2% for Nvidia.
The valuation distinction comes down to certainty versus optionality. Nvidia commands the premium because it owns the established ecosystem. AMD can offer greater upside if accelerator share rises materially, but investors are underwriting a competitive outcome that has not yet been fully achieved.
The record TSM numbers support both companies' demand outlooks, but Nvidia remains better positioned to absorb higher supply-chain costs. AMD is the higher-beta bet that hyperscaler demand for a second accelerator platform becomes large enough to overwhelm that margin disadvantage.
